source.title: Revisiting Weak-to-Strong Generalization in Theory and Practice: Reverse KL vs. Forward KL
source.authors: Wei Yao; Wen-Kai Yang; Ziqiao Wang; Yankai Lin; Yong Liu

record.tranche_reason: The study fine-tunes stronger models using weaker-model supervision and evaluates task accuracy, including standard CE as a weak-to-strong baseline; it also compares alternative losses in this setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-accuracy results for weak-to-strong training, comparisons against weak supervisors, loss comparisons, noise experiments, and theoretical bounds. Figure-based GPT-2 and Pythia values are not numerically transcribed because the text gives aggregate comparisons rather than exact plotted values. It discusses Burns et al.'s confidence regularization, but does not provide exact plotted values for that comparison.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes stronger GPT-2, Pythia and Qwen2.5 reward models on weaker models' labels (the Burns et al. recipe) and compares them with the weak supervisor. It also compares reverse KL and reverse CE losses against forward KL and CE, varies model sizes, and proves conditions under which the student beats its supervisor.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that reverse KL and reverse CE beat forward KL and CE in most settings and tolerate noise better, with reverse KL degrading under extreme noise. Their theoretical guarantee (the student beats the weak supervisor by their disagreement) requires reverse KL, a convex last-layer function class and a realizable strong representation. They acknowledge these assumptions may not hold for LLMs.
record.recipe_differences: Uses weak-model labels to fine-tune stronger models and measures test accuracy, but systematically compares reverse KL/reverse CE with forward KL/CE rather than reproducing only the original standard-CE recipe; experiments use reward-modeling classification.
record.method_sensitivity: Loss choice; weak-teacher and strong-student size; model family; dataset/task; amount of swapped weak-label noise.
record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: PGR is not calculated. GPT-2 and Pythia results are mostly presented in figures without exact values in the prose; the noise table experiments are each run once. The authors note that their experiments use two binary alignment datasets and relatively smaller models, and that the assumptions behind the theoretical results may not hold in practice.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 reports three teacher-student settings, four loss variants, and five noise levels. To stay within the row limit while retaining each loss comparison at the most extreme stated noise level, only the 50% noise rows are included; the 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40% entries are omitted. Exact individual GPT-2 and Pythia figure values and Figure 3 confidence-regularization values are also not transcribed because the text gives no exact numbers for them.

untested.parts: PGR is never computed. Weak-supervisor and ceiling values for Qwen are not reported. Per-setting GPT-2 and Pythia values appear only in figures.
Ensembling of weak supervisors is not tested. The Burns confidence loss is tested only as a carrier for reverse CE.
No PGR scaling, no chess or NLP-classification tasks, and no representation-based predictors.
Not tested: exploitation, distribution shift and correlated errors.

missing.what: Confidence-regularized CE vs reverse confidence-regularized CE: the reverse version consistently outperforms, and confidence loss modestly improves over plain CE.
Pythia strong ceiling outperforms GPT-2 ceiling; the authors link a stronger weak model to smaller reverse-loss gains.

record.verdict_notes: Accuracy is the measure throughout; no PGR is reported. Qwen gains are tiny and mostly within the SDs. The record keeps only the 50% noise level, where all methods are near or below chance. That understates the 10–40% results in Table 2, where reverse losses beat forward in most cells; the exceptions are Base→Large at 10% and Medium→Large RCE at 10%. Mirror rows (R12, R14, R16, R18, R20, R22) duplicate their paired rows and are unlinked. Noise is deliberately injected, which is acceptable as a robustness condition for V2.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not calculate PGR or quantify the recovered fraction of the strong-ceiling gap; the reported empirical comparison is task accuracy versus the weak supervisor.
It compares reverse and forward KL/CE losses, including a confidence-regularization variant, but does not test ensembling weak supervisors or other loss variants.
It varies model sizes/families and evaluates helpfulness and harmlessness reward-modeling settings, but does not report PGR, chess results, or empirical predictors based on representations.

No test of student exploitation of what a weak supervisor cannot check, distribution shift, or gains shrinking when weak and strong models err alike. Its injected label-noise experiments are recorded under V2.
Theoretical conditions are analyzed for reverse KL and reverse CE; no empirical verification of those theoretical conditions is reported.
No vision or other non-language modality experiment.

rows.subject: Reverse-KL weak-to-strong setting with convex function class and realizable strong representation
rows.stage_stated: Last-linear-layer fine-tuning is the motivating case; formal result assumes a convex function class
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical analysis of minimizing reverse KL to weak-model predictions

conditions.value: Convex function class; strong representation can realize the ground-truth function

rows.measure: Strong-model generalization error relative to weak-model error
rows.value: KL(F⋆, Fsw) ≤ KL(F⋆, Fw) − KL(Fsw, Fw)
rows.note: Conditional theoretical guarantee: the student improves over the weak model by at least their disagreement.
rows.check: V1 link removed: a theorem is not an empirical V1 result.

rows.subject: Empirical reverse-KL weak-to-strong setting
rows.operation_detail: Finite-sample theoretical analysis of empirical reverse-KL fine-tuning

conditions.value: Convex function class; n i.i.d. samples; strong-ceiling generalization error ε

rows.measure: Strong-model generalization error relative to weak-model error
rows.value: KL(F⋆, F̂sw) ≤ KL(F⋆, Fw) − KL(F̂sw, Fw) + O(√ε) + O(√(CFs/n)) + O(√(log(1/δ)/n))
rows.note: The guarantee includes finite-sample and ceiling-error remainder terms, which the authors say diminish as sample size increases and ε becomes small.
rows.check: V1 link removed.

rows.subject: Reverse-CE weak-to-strong setting
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical analysis of reverse cross-entropy fine-tuning

conditions.value: Convex function class; strong representation realizes the ground truth

rows.measure: Strong-model cross-entropy error relative to weak-model error
rows.value: CE(F⋆, Fsw) ≤ 1/2(CE(F⋆, Fw) − KL(Fsw, Fw)) + log k
rows.note: The bound includes a log k term; the authors describe it as suggesting probable improvement, particularly for binary classification.
rows.check: V1 link removed. With k=2, log 2 ≈ 0.69 is not obviously negligible, and the 1/2 factor is present. The bound does not strictly guarantee improvement.

relation.reason: Its own experiments compare students with weak supervisors and alternative losses, and its theorems establish conditional improvement bounds.

tranche.reason: The study systematically changes the training objective to reverse KL and reverse CE to address the same weak-to-strong question. Forward-loss baselines accompany a different-method test.

source_check.notes: PGR is not reported; fixed-pair accuracy comparisons establish loss rankings, while cross-size accuracy trends do not establish PGR trends. ACL review metadata is not verifiable from the supplied paper text.

statements.correction: Corollary 2 assumes a convex function class and realizability. Its bound is CE(F⋆,Fsw) ≤ ½[CE(F⋆,Fw) − KL(Fsw,Fw)] + log k.
statements.problem: The bound is correct, but the conditions wording can imply that this study's reverse-CE result dispenses with convexity.
